head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The largest position flipped so far
If the first `step` bits are all 1 and nothing beyond is, the largest flipped position is exactly `step`
Gives the step number (1, 2, 3, ...) with each flipped position
After step flips, the largest flipped position equals step
flips is a permutation, so step distinct positions all at most step are exactly 1..step

1375.takeaway: Because flips is a permutation, the string is prefix-aligned exactly when the largest flipped position equals the number of steps taken.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Maximum value: turn the first digit that is not 9 into 9 (everywhere it appears)
Largest number greedily maximises from the left
Replaces every copy of that digit
Replace the first digit by 1 everywhere
Instead replace the first later digit that is not 0 or 1 with 0
The leading 1 must stay; digits 0 and 1 are already as small as allowed

head: Variable
Computation
Value
rows: first non-9 digit is 5 → every 5 becomes 9

blocks.h: Why replacing with 0 is only allowed after a leading 1
p: Changing the first digit to 0 would give a leading zero, which is not allowed. So the first digit goes to 1 when it can. When it already is 1, the next best option is to turn some other digit into 0 (digits 0 and 1 are skipped because changing them either does nothing or would damage the leading 1).

1432.takeaway: Greedy on digits: make the biggest value by turning the first non-9 into 9, and the smallest by turning the first digit into 1 (or a later digit into 0 if it already is 1).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Best dot product using prefixes nums1[:i], nums2[:j] with at least one pair
Marks 'no valid pair yet', so empty subsequences are never chosen
Dot product if we pair just these two elements
Skip an element from either array
Pair them and extend a previous result only if it helps (a negative previous result is dropped)

p: `dp[3][3] = 18`, built from `2 × 3 + (-2) × (-6)`. The last row cannot beat it: pairing 5 with a later element only gives `-24` at best, so `dp[4][3] = 18`.

1458.takeaway: Subsequence DP with four options per cell: skip from either side, pair alone, or pair and extend a previous result when it is positive.

head: Code
What it does

rows: Moves to the last node that will be kept (the m-th)
Skips n nodes (or until the list ends)
Links the kept part to what comes after the deleted part and continues from there

bullets: Time: O(L) for a list of L nodes.

1474.takeaway: Walk m−1 steps to the last kept node, skip n nodes, relink, and repeat.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: All index triples i < j < k
n ≤ 100, so about 160,000 triples is cheap
Counts the triples that satisfy them

p: `arr = [3,0,1,1,9,7]`, `a = 7, b = 2, c = 3`. The good triples are:

blocks.h: Why no triple with 9 or 7 works
p: For example `(0,4,5)` (3, 9, 7) fails the last check: `|3 − 7| = 4 > 3`. The others using 9 or 7 fail the first or last check as well. The total is 4.

1534.takeaway: With n up to 100, checking every triple directly is fast enough.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The first element is always the root of the BST
Elements smaller / larger than the root, in their original order
Ways to interleave the left and right sequences: choose which positions go to the left group
Left and right subtrees are independent of each other
Times the ways inside each subtree
Arrays of length 0, 1 or 2 have only one valid order

p: For `[3,4,5,1,2]`: root 3, left `[1,2]`, right `[4,5]`. `comb(4, 2) = 6` interleavings, subtrees contribute 1 each, so 6 − 1 = 5.

bullets: Time: O(n²) in the worst case (splitting lists at each level).

1569.takeaway: The root must come first; the two subtrees keep their own order and can be interleaved in C(n−1, left size) ways, times the ways inside each.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The neighbouring characters (empty at the edges)
Only two neighbours can block, so one of three always works
Picks the first letter different from both

p: `ubv?w`: the `?` has neighbours `v` and `w`, so `a` is picked and the result is `ubvaw`. If the right neighbour is another `?`, it will be replaced later and will avoid the letter chosen here.

1576.takeaway: Each '?' has at most two neighbours, so trying 'a', 'b', 'c' always finds a letter that differs from both.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The earlier prefix remainder such that the subarray between has sum ≡ r (mod p)
Maps a prefix remainder to the latest index where it occurred (starts with {0: -1})
Latest index gives the shortest subarray
Removing the whole array is not allowed, so best starts at n and stays n if nothing shorter is found

p: Best is 1: remove the element 4, leaving `3 + 1 + 2 = 6`, divisible by 6.

1590.takeaway: Find the shortest subarray whose sum has the same remainder as the total, using prefix remainders in a hash map.

No point can lie strictly inside the widest empty vertical strip between neighbouring x-values

1637.takeaway: Ignore y, sort the x-coordinates, and return the largest gap between neighbours.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: An upper bound so the search ends: past max(forbidden, x) + a + b going further right cannot help
Position, whether the last jump was backward, and the jumps used
The no-two-backward rule needs that flag
Explores by number of jumps, so the first time pos == x is the minimum
Forward is always allowed; backward only if the last jump was not backward

1654.takeaway: BFS on (position, last-jump-was-backward) states with a bounded range finds the fewest jumps.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Make every number even first (odd numbers doubled)
Doubling an odd number is its only upward move; afterwards only halving remains
Smallest element currently in the heap
The largest is odd and cannot be halved, so the maximum cannot be reduced further
Halve the maximum (the only way to shrink the range) and update low

bullets: Time: O(n log n + n log M) where M is the largest value.

1675.takeaway: Raise every odd number once, then repeatedly halve the maximum with a heap; the deviation is checked after each step until the maximum is odd.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Removes the gaps the ones must keep between each other: ones become adjacent when all p values are equal
Turns 'make them consecutive' into 'make them equal'
Each window of k consecutive ones is considered
The median minimises the total distance
Sum of |p − med| for the left half and the right half, using prefix sums

p: The best window costs 1: swap the 0 between the last two ones to make them adjacent.

1703.takeaway: Subtract each one's index to remove the required gaps, then the cost of gathering k ones is the sum of distances to the median, computed with prefix sums.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Joins the two indices of each allowed swap
Swaps chain: connected indices can be arranged in any order
Multiset overlap: how many values can be matched inside the group

p: Matches total 3, so the Hamming distance is `4 − 3 = 1`.

1722.takeaway: Indices joined by swaps form groups where values can be rearranged freely; count how many values already match as multisets.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Each user's languages as a set
A friend pair with no shared language
Users who are in at least one such pair
How many users in need already know each language
Teach the most-known language to everyone in need who lacks it
Only one language may be taught

p: `need = {user 1, user 2}`; language 1 is known by user 1 and language 2 by user 2, so the best count is 1. Teaching one language to the other user costs `2 − 1 = 1`.

1733.takeaway: Only friend pairs without a shared language matter; pick the language already known by most of those users and teach the rest.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: All water cells start the search together (multi-source BFS)

blocks.h: Result and why it is the best
p: The grid becomes `[[1,0],[2,1]]`. Each land cell gets its distance to the nearest water cell: it cannot be higher because neighbours differ by at most 1, and BFS gives the largest legal height.

1765.takeaway: Heights are the distance to the nearest water cell, found with one BFS started from all water cells at once.
